speaker: Host (Alice)
text: Hey everyone, welcome back to Fusion Frontiers! I'm Alice, your host.

speaker: Host (Alice)
text: Today, we're cracking open a hot topic—literally!—about fusion reactors.

speaker: Host (Alice)
text: Joining me is Dr. Beom Seok Kim from the National Fusion Research Institute.

speaker: Host (Alice)
text: Dr. Kim, thanks for being here. Ready to talk about radioactive leftovers?

speaker: Guest
text: Absolutely, Alice. It's not the most glamorous part, but it's super important.

speaker: Host (Alice)
text: So, fusion gets called 'clean energy' all the time. Is that the whole story?

speaker: Guest
text: Well, it's cleaner than fission, but fusion still leaves behind some radioactive materials.

speaker: Host (Alice)
text: What actually gets radioactive inside a fusion reactor like K-DEMO?

speaker: Guest
text: Mostly the parts inside the reactor—the blankets and divertors—get hit by fusion neutrons.

speaker: Host (Alice)
text: And when you say 'activated,' what does that mean for those parts?

speaker: Guest
text: It means they soak up neutrons and become radioactive themselves, giving off decay heat.

speaker: Host (Alice)
text: So, even after you shut down the reactor, it's still hot in there?

speaker: Guest
text: Exactly! It's like when you turn off your oven, but it stays hot for ages.

speaker: Host (Alice)
text: How much heat are we talking about after, say, two years of running K-DEMO?

speaker: Guest
text: After shutdown, the blankets and divertors can give off around 63 megawatts of heat.

speaker: Host (Alice)
text: Whoa, that's like running a small power plant just in leftovers!

speaker: Guest
text: Yeah, it's a lot! If you don't cool them, some modules could hit 1300°C. Not good.

speaker: Host (Alice)
text: Yikes! So, cooling isn't just a nice-to-have—it's a must, right?

speaker: Guest
text: Definitely. Without cooling, you risk damaging the reactor and making maintenance impossible.

speaker: Host (Alice)
text: How long does it take for things to cool down to a safer temperature?

speaker: Guest
text: With natural convection, it takes about 10 days to get down to 200°C.

speaker: Host (Alice)
text: Ten days! That's a long wait for anyone wanting to get inside and fix things.

speaker: Guest
text: Exactly. And even then, the radioactivity means only robots can go in for a while.

speaker: Host (Alice)
text: So, what happens if the cooling system fails? Is it like a kitchen disaster?

speaker: Guest
text: Pretty much! Imagine leaving a roast in the oven with the door shut—things get messy fast.

speaker: Host (Alice)
text: You mentioned regulations. How does Korea decide if this waste is safe to bury?

speaker: Guest
text: We check if it's low-level waste. If it is, it can go to shallow land burial sites safely.

speaker: Host (Alice)
text: Are there any elements that keep you up at night?

speaker: Guest
text: Long-lived ones like carbon-14 and cobalt-60, but in K-DEMO, they're below the safety limits.

speaker: Host (Alice)
text: That's a relief! So, is fusion still safer than fission when it comes to waste?

speaker: Guest
text: Yes, overall. Fusion waste is less dangerous and easier to manage, but it still needs care.

speaker: Host (Alice)
text: Can you recycle or reuse any of these radioactive parts?

speaker: Guest
text: Absolutely! Recycling helps cut down waste and makes maintenance smoother.

speaker: Host (Alice)
text: If you could bust one myth about fusion, what would it be?

speaker: Guest
text: That fusion is totally clean. It's cleaner, but not spotless—there's still some waste.

speaker: Host (Alice)
text: Looking ahead, how will your research help future reactors?

speaker: Guest
text: It helps us design better cooling and safer maintenance, making fusion more practical.

speaker: Host (Alice)
text: So, fusion's future is bright, but we need to be smart about heat and waste.

speaker: Guest
text: Exactly. With good planning, fusion can be a safe, sustainable energy source.

speaker: Host (Alice)
text: Dr. Kim, this was eye-opening—and a little spicy! Thanks for joining us.

speaker: Guest
text: Thank you, Alice. Always happy to talk about the hot side of fusion!

speaker: Host (Alice)
text: And thanks to our listeners. Stay curious, and catch us next time on Fusion Frontiers!
